summary: Describes version two of Microsoft's PPP CHAP dialect, which is similar to but incompatible with version one. It documents a vendor challenge-based authentication method. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Proving who you are by answering a secret challenge instead of telling the secret itself. This is Microsoft's second version.

questions: how does microsoft chap version 2 work
how does ms-chap v2 mutual authentication work
what is the difference between ms-chap v1 and v2
subtitle: Microsoft's second PPP CHAP dialect, which adds mutual authentication so the server must prove itself too.

tldr.problem: Version one of Microsoft's CHAP dialect only let the server check the user. The user had no proof that the server knew the password, and some fields in the version one packets needed rework.
tldr.mechanism: MS-CHAP-V2 piggybacks a peer challenge on the Response packet and an authenticator response on the Success packet, so each side proves it knows the password. It is negotiated as CHAP Algorithm 0x81 in LCP.
tldr.outcome: It is similar to but incompatible with MS-CHAP-V1, and it adds a Change-Password packet. The memo is Informational and does not define an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2759 is an Informational memo and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents a vendor-specific dialect rather than an Internet standard; version one of the dialect is described in RFC 2433.

sections.title: What MS-CHAP-V2 Changes
sections.content:
RFC 2759 describes version two of Microsoft's dialect of the PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP), called MS-CHAP-V2. Where possible it stays consistent with both MS-CHAP-V1 (described in RFC 2433) and standard CHAP (RFC 1994), but it is incompatible with version one: certain fields were deleted or reused with different meanings.

The RFC lists the main differences. MS-CHAP-V2 is enabled by negotiating CHAP Algorithm 0x81 in LCP option 3, Authentication Protocol. It adds mutual authentication. The Windows NT compatible challenge response now includes the peer challenge and the user name. The LAN Manager compatible response is replaced by the Peer-Challenge field. The Failure message format changed, and the two old Change Password packets are replaced by a single Change-Password packet.

The LCP setup is identical to standard CHAP except that the Algorithm field is 0x81 instead of the MD5 value 0x05. A PPP implementation that does not know MS-CHAP-V2 but correctly implements LCP Config-Rej should have no problem rejecting this non-standard option.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of a way to prove who you are. The big new thing is that the computer you call has to prove itself to you as well.

sections.title: Challenge and Response Packets
sections.content:
The Challenge packet has the same format as a standard CHAP Challenge. The authenticator sends a 16-octet challenge Value. Implementations need not copy Microsoft's way of choosing it, but the standard guidelines on randomness SHOULD be followed. Microsoft authenticators do not currently fill in the Name field.

The Response packet also has the standard CHAP format, but its Value field is split into four parts: a 16-octet Peer-Challenge, 8 reserved octets that must be zero, a 24-octet NT-Response and a 1-octet Flags field that MUST be zero.

The peer makes up the Peer-Challenge itself as a random number. The NT-Response is computed from the password, the user name, the Peer-Challenge and the challenge it received. Only the user name is used in that calculation, without any Windows NT domain name, even if a domain prefix such as BIGCO\johndoe appears in the Name field.

The RFC notes that a Windows NT password is a string of 0 to (theoretically) 256 case-sensitive Unicode characters, and that current versions of Windows NT limit passwords to 14 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks a random puzzle. The caller adds a random puzzle of its own, mixes both with the secret and sends back the answer. Now both puzzles are in play.

sections.title: Success and Failure Packets
sections.content:
The Success packet carries a Message of the form S=<auth_string> M=<message>. The auth string is a 20-octet number written as 40 hexadecimal digits (A to F in uppercase), computed from the challenge, the Peer-Challenge, the NT-Response and the password. This is how the server proves it knows the password. The peer MUST verify it, and if it is missing or wrong the peer MUST end the session.

The Failure packet is unusual: contrary to standard CHAP, its Message text affects how the protocol runs. The format is E=eeeeeeeeee R=r C=cccc... V=vvvvvvvvvv M=<msg>. E is a decimal error code, R is 1 if a retry is allowed and 0 if not, C is a new challenge that MUST be exactly 32 octets of hexadecimal text, and V is the password-change version, which SHOULD always be 3 for MS-CHAP-V2. When R=1 the authenticator disables short timeouts, expecting the peer to prompt the user for new credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server says yes, it also shows a secret handshake only the real server could know. When it says no, it says why and whether you may try again.

sections.title: Retries and Changing a Password
sections.content:
The Change-Password packet exists in neither standard CHAP nor MS-CHAP-V1. It lets the peer change the password on the account named in the preceding Response, and it should be sent only if the Failure packet reported ERROR_PASSWD_EXPIRED (E=648). The RFC says recent versions of Windows NT 4.0, Windows 95 and Windows 98 support it, while Windows NT 3.5, Windows NT 3.51 and early versions of the others do not.

The packet uses Code 7 and has a Length of 586. Its fields are the new password encrypted with the old password hash (516 octets), the old hash encrypted with the new hash (16 octets), a Peer-Challenge, 8 reserved octets, an NT-Response calculated on the new password and the challenge from the Failure packet, and 2 flag octets that are all reserved. The Identifier is the Failure packet's Identifier plus 1.

The RFC walks through example exchanges: success on the first try, failure with no retry, success after a retry, a failed guessing attack that gets 3 attempts, and success with a password change. The packet sequence ID goes up on each retry response and on the change password response. A response retry is never allowed after Change Password, but Change Password may follow a retry.
sections.plainLanguage: If your password has run out, you can send a new one, wrapped up in a locked box that only the old password can open. You may try again after a mistake, but only a few times.

sections.title: How the Values Are Computed
sections.content:
Section 8 gives pseudocode for every field. To make the NT-Response, ChallengeHash() runs SHA-1 over the Peer-Challenge, the authenticator challenge and the user name, and keeps the first 8 octets as the Challenge. NtPasswordHash() hashes the password with MD4 into 16 octets. ChallengeResponse() zero-pads that hash to 21 octets, splits it into three 7-octet keys and uses each as a DES key to encrypt the 8-octet Challenge, giving a 24-octet response.

For the authenticator response, the password hash is hashed again with MD4, then run through SHA-1 together with the NT-Response and a constant string (Magic1, 39 octets), and then through SHA-1 again with the Challenge and a second constant (Magic2, 41 octets). The result is written as S= plus 40 hexadecimal digits. The peer builds the same value and compares it.

The Change-Password fields use RC4 and DES. The RFC also provides a worked hash example for the user name User and password clientPass, and an example of turning 7-octet hash pieces into DES keys with odd parity.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is made by scrambling the secret, the two puzzles and the user name together in a fixed recipe. Both sides know the recipe, so both can check the other's result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single sentence. As an implementation detail, the authenticator SHOULD limit the number of password retries allowed, to make brute-force password guessing attacks more difficult. The example of a failed attack in the RFC allows 3 attempts before the server sends R=0.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let someone keep guessing the password forever. After a few wrong tries, say no.

messages.label: Success / Authenticator Response
messages.note: The peer verifies it, then the call continues.
